active_paradigms.description: Apply scipy.signal.savgol_filter directly to the input signal with polynomial order 2-3 and window size based on the input parameter. Unlike Gaussian smoothing which blurs the signal, Savitzky-Golay fits local polynomials to preserve signal shape and derivative information while smoothing. This reduces slope changes by filtering noise-induced reversals while maintaining responsiveness to genuine trend changes. The polynomial fitting inherently preserves signal dynamics better than simple smoothing. Use mode='interp' or 'nearest' for edge handling to minimize boundary artifacts.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Slope changes (S) and false reversals (R) while maintaining low lag error through derivative preservation
active_paradigms.cautions: Polynomial order should be 2 or 3 (higher orders cause oscillations), window size must be odd, ensure window_size parameter is properly converted to odd integer

active_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.ndimage.binary_dilation for derivative-based hysteresis filtering
active_paradigms.description: Compute the derivative of the signal, then apply binary thresholding to identify significant slope changes. Use scipy.ndimage.binary_dilation or binary_erosion to implement hysteresis logic that suppresses small noise-induced reversals while preserving larger genuine trend changes. The morphological operations create a dead zone around zero crossings that filters rapid direction changes below a threshold. Integrate the filtered derivative back to reconstruct the signal. This approach explicitly targets the slope change penalty by implementing a noise-aware reversal detection mechanism.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Slope changes (S) and false reversals (R) through explicit noise-aware reversal suppression
active_paradigms.cautions: Threshold selection is critical - too high loses genuine changes, too low doesn't filter noise; use adaptive thresholding based on signal variance; ensure proper integration with original signal's starting value

active_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.signal.lfilter with custom IIR coefficients for zero-phase lag filtering
active_paradigms.description: Design custom Butterworth or Chebyshev IIR filter coefficients using scipy.signal.butter or scipy.signal.cheby1, then apply with scipy.signal.lfilter in forward-only mode to minimize phase delay. Unlike smoothing filters that introduce significant lag, IIR filters can be designed with specific frequency responses that attenuate high-frequency noise while preserving low-frequency trends with minimal phase shift. The filter cutoff frequency should be tuned based on the window_size parameter to balance noise reduction and responsiveness. This approach directly addresses lag error while still providing noise suppression.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Lag error (L_recent, L_avg) while maintaining slope change reduction through frequency-selective filtering
active_paradigms.cautions: Must use forward-only filtering to minimize lag (not filtfilt which introduces delay), carefully tune cutoff frequency relative to signal characteristics, ensure filter stability with proper coefficient selection

tried_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.interpolate.interp1d with cubic spline for signal reconstruction
tried_paradigms.description: Apply scipy.interpolate.interp1d with cubic spline interpolation to reconstruct the signal from a downsampled version. First, decimate the signal by selecting every N-th sample (where N is based on window_size), then use cubic spline interpolation to reconstruct at original resolution. This approach acts as a low-pass filter by removing high-frequency noise components while preserving the overall signal shape. The cubic spline provides smooth interpolation that naturally minimizes slope changes. Unlike traditional filters, this is a reconstruction-based approach that can handle non-uniform sampling effects and provides excellent phase characteristics with minimal lag.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Minimize lag error (L_recent) while reducing slope changes through smooth reconstruction
tried_paradigms.cautions: Ensure the decimation factor is appropriate for the signal bandwidth. May need to handle edge cases carefully to avoid extrapolation artifacts.

tried_paradigms.description: Apply scipy.ndimage.median_filter before the derivative-smoothing-integration pipeline to remove noise spikes that cause false reversals. Median filtering is robust to outliers and preserves signal edges better than mean-based filters. The key is to apply median filtering with an appropriate window size (typically 3-7 samples) to suppress high-frequency noise while maintaining signal dynamics. This pre-processing step removes extreme values that would otherwise create spurious slope changes in the derivative. Combine this with the existing derivative-smoothing approach for dual-layer protection against false reversals.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: False reversals (R) and slope changes (S) by removing outlier-induced directional changes before derivative computation
tried_paradigms.cautions: Choose median window size carefully - too small won't remove noise, too large will over-smooth and increase lag. Test odd window sizes like 3, 5, 7 for best results.

tried_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.signal.wiener for adaptive noise estimation
tried_paradigms.description: Apply scipy.signal.wiener filter which estimates local signal-to-noise ratio and adapts smoothing strength accordingly. The Wiener filter computes local mean and variance in a sliding window, then applies optimal linear filtering based on the estimated noise characteristics. This provides adaptive smoothing - more aggressive in noisy regions, less in clean regions. Use with a window size parameter (typically 5-15) to control the adaptation scale. This directly addresses the trade-off between noise reduction and tracking accuracy by adapting to local signal conditions.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Balance between L_avg (tracking error) and S (slope changes) through adaptive smoothing that responds to local noise levels
tried_paradigms.cautions: Wiener filter assumes locally stationary statistics - may struggle with rapidly changing noise characteristics. Ensure window_size is appropriate for signal frequency content.

tried_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.interpolate.splrep and scipy.interpolate.splev for spline-based smoothing
tried_paradigms.description: Fit a cubic spline to the noisy signal using scipy.interpolate.splrep with a smoothing parameter (s), then evaluate at original sample points using scipy.interpolate.splev. The smoothing parameter controls the trade-off between fitting the data exactly (s=0) and producing a smooth curve (larger s). This approach preserves signal structure while removing high-frequency noise through mathematical smoothing rather than filtering. Choose s based on signal characteristics - larger s for noisier signals, smaller s for cleaner signals. The spline naturally produces smooth derivatives, reducing slope change penalties.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Slope changes (S) and false reversals (R) through mathematically smooth signal reconstruction with controlled smoothing parameter
tried_paradigms.cautions: The smoothing parameter s is critical - use cross-validation or heuristic based on noise level. Too small s overfits noise, too large s loses signal dynamics. Start with s = n * noise_variance as a heuristic.

tried_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.optimize.minimize with slope change penalty as constrained optimization
tried_paradigms.description: Formulate signal filtering as a constrained optimization problem where the objective function directly minimizes tracking error plus an explicit penalty term for slope changes. The objective is: sum((y - x)^2) + lambda * sum((diff(diff(y)))^2). Use scipy.optimize.minimize with SLSQP method to find the optimal filtered signal that balances tracking accuracy against slope smoothness. The regularization parameter lambda directly controls the trade-off between following the noisy signal and maintaining smooth derivatives. This approach directly targets the slope change metric (alpha=0.3) and false reversal penalty (alpha=0.3) which together account for 60% of the score.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Directly minimize slope changes and false reversals while maintaining tracking accuracy. Tune lambda to balance smoothness vs responsiveness.
tried_paradigms.cautions: Optimizing a 500+ element vector can be slow - use good initial guess (e.g., simple smoothed signal). Set appropriate bounds to prevent divergence. May need to reduce signal length or use coarser optimization grid. Ensure filtered signal length matches input exactly.

tried_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.optimize.least_squares with Huber loss for robust regression
tried_paradigms.description: Apply robust regression using scipy.optimize.least_squares with Huber loss function to fit a smooth model to the noisy signal. The Huber loss is less sensitive to outliers than L2 loss, making it more robust to noise-induced spikes that cause false reversals. Model the signal as a low-degree polynomial or use a basis function approach where the optimization finds coefficients that minimize Huber loss. The robustness of Huber loss naturally suppresses noise-induced directional changes while preserving genuine trend changes. This approach targets the false reversal penalty by being less reactive to noise spikes.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Reduce false reversals caused by noise outliers while maintaining tracking of genuine trends. The Huber loss threshold parameter controls sensitivity to outliers.
tried_paradigms.cautions: Need to define an appropriate model/basis for the signal. The Huber threshold parameter must be tuned based on expected noise level. Ensure the model is flexible enough to capture signal dynamics but constrained enough to avoid overfitting noise.

tried_paradigms.idea: Derivative-smoothing-integration with median filter for robustness
tried_paradigms.description: Improve the current derivative-smoothing-integration approach by replacing the Gaussian filter with a median filter on the derivative. The median filter is more robust to outliers and preserves edges better than Gaussian smoothing, which directly addresses false reversals caused by noise spikes. Compute the first derivative using np.diff, apply scipy.ndimage.median_filter with window_size tuned to the noise characteristics, then integrate back using np.cumsum starting from the original signal's first value. This maintains the proven derivative-smoothing framework while improving robustness to noise-induced reversals.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Reduce false reversals while maintaining the benefits of derivative-smoothing-integration. The median filter's window size controls the trade-off between noise suppression and responsiveness.
tried_paradigms.cautions: Median filter may introduce slight nonlinearity compared to Gaussian. The window size must be carefully chosen - too small won't suppress noise, too large will lag genuine changes. Ensure proper handling of edge effects with appropriate mode parameter.

tried_paradigms.idea: Hysteresis-based directional filter for false reversal suppression
tried_paradigms.description: Implement a custom hysteresis filter that tracks the signal's direction and only accepts a reversal when the change exceeds a minimum threshold. The algorithm maintains a running 'trend direction' state and requires a significant deviation (e.g., 2x the local noise estimate) before flipping the direction. This directly targets the R(θ) false reversal penalty by preventing noise-induced direction changes while allowing genuine trend reversals. The filter processes the signal sequentially, computing local noise estimates from recent samples and using them to dynamically adjust the hysteresis threshold. Output is the smoothed signal with suppressed spurious reversals.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: False reversal penalty R(θ) and slope change count S(θ) - these together weight 0.6 of the composite score
tried_paradigms.cautions: Hysteresis threshold must be adaptive to handle varying noise levels; too high causes lag, too low allows false reversals; ensure output length matches input

tried_paradigms.description: Use scipy.signal.savgol_filter which fits local polynomials via least squares to smooth the signal while preserving important features like peaks and slopes. Unlike Gaussian filtering which blurs features, Savitzky-Golay maintains signal shape characteristics. Set the window size based on the input window_size parameter and use polynomial order 2 or 3 for optimal balance between smoothness and responsiveness. This approach directly reduces slope changes by smoothing the signal while maintaining trend accuracy, addressing both S(θ) and L_avg(θ) simultaneously.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Slope changes S(θ) and tracking accuracy (correlation with clean signal) - preserves genuine trends while removing noise-induced reversals
tried_paradigms.cautions: Window size must be odd; polynomial order affects responsiveness; edge handling needs careful attention to avoid artifacts

tried_paradigms.idea: Adaptive exponential moving average with volatility-based smoothing
tried_paradigms.description: Implement an adaptive EMA where the smoothing factor α is dynamically adjusted based on local signal volatility. Compute local volatility as the standard deviation of recent differences; when volatility is high (signal changing rapidly), use higher α (less smoothing, more responsiveness); when volatility is low (stable signal), use lower α (more smoothing). This creates a self-adapting filter that naturally balances lag and smoothness. The EMA is computed as y[n] = α*x[n] + (1-α)*y[n-1], with α ranging from 0.1 to 0.5 based on volatility. This directly targets the L_recent(θ) lag error while maintaining acceptable S(θ).
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Lag error L_recent(θ) and average tracking error L_avg(θ) - adaptive smoothing reduces lag during rapid changes while smoothing during stable periods
tried_paradigms.cautions: Volatility window size affects adaptation speed; ensure α bounds prevent instability; handle initial conditions properly
